question: In the low-field drift model, μn=1000 cm²/(V·s) and E=+100 V/cm. Find the signed electron drift velocity along x in cm/s.

steps: Electrons have negative charge and drift opposite to the field.
Multiply mobility by field: 1000×100=10⁵ cm/s.
Include the direction sign to obtain −10⁵ cm/s.
solution.explanation: Include the direction sign to obtain −10⁵ cm/s.
commonMistakes: Conventional electron current points opposite to electron particle drift.

hints: Identify the conditions under which electron drift direction applies.
Start from $ v_{dn}=-\mu_nE $.

verification.method: Low-field particle drift with negative electron charge sign. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.

question: A semiconductor has n=p=5×10¹⁴ cm⁻³, μn=2000 and μp=400 cm²/(V·s). At E=10 V/cm, find total drift current density in A/cm² using q=1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C.

solution.asked: Add electron and hole conventional drift currents.
steps: The weighted carrier mobility sum is 5×10¹⁴(2000+400)=1.2×10¹⁸.
Multiplying by q gives conductivity 0.192 S/cm.
Multiplying by E=10 V/cm gives J=1.92 A/cm².
solution.explanation: Multiplying by E=10 V/cm gives J=1.92 A/cm².
commonMistakes: Electron and hole drift currents add in the conventional current reference despite opposite particle drifts.

hints: Identify the conditions under which two-carrier drift conductivity applies.
Start from $ J=q(n\mu_n+p\mu_p)E $.

verification.method: Sum two conventional carrier-current contributions in centimeter units. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.

question: Minority carriers have diffusion coefficient D=25 cm²/s and lifetime τ=4 μs. Find the diffusion length in μm.

steps: Taking its square root gives 10⁻² cm.
Multiplying by 10⁴ μm/cm gives 100 μm.
commonMistakes: Lifetime must be in seconds before multiplication by a cm²/s coefficient.

hints: Identify the conditions under which diffusion length applies.
Start from $ L=\sqrt{D\tau} $.

verification.method: Solve L²=Dτ and convert centimeters to micrometers. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.

question: Uniform excess carriers obey dΔn/dt=−Δn/τ after illumination stops. With τ=2 μs, find the time at which the excess density falls to one quarter, in μs.

steps: Set the decay factor to 1/4.
Taking logarithms gives t=τln4.
commonMistakes: A quarter density is reached after two half-lives, not a quarter of one lifetime.

question: Uniform steady photogeneration is G=10²⁰ cm⁻³s⁻¹ and the linear excess-carrier lifetime is 1 μs. Ignoring transport, find the excess steady density in units of 10¹⁴ cm⁻³.

steps: No spatial transport or time variation remains under the stated assumptions.

question: A hole concentration decreases in the +x direction with zero electric field. The conventional hole diffusion current points:

options.text: In a direction independent of the concentration gradient

solution.asked: Find the sign of hole diffusion current.
steps: Particles diffuse from higher to lower concentration, here in +x.
Holes carry positive charge, so their conventional current has that same direction.
The formula also gives a positive value when dp/dx<0, so A is correct.
solution.explanation: The formula also gives a positive value when dp/dx<0, so A is correct.
commonMistakes: A zero electric field removes drift, not diffusion.

hints: Identify the conditions under which hole diffusion sign applies.
Start from $ J_{p,diff}=-qD_p\frac{dp}{dx} $.

verification.method: Fick particle flux down the density gradient, times positive hole charge. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.

question: For p(x)=p0+10¹⁵exp(−x/0.001) cm⁻³ with x in cm, Dp=10 cm²/s and q=1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, find Jp,diff(0) in A/cm².

solution.asked: Differentiate the profile and calculate current.
steps: At x=0, dp/dx=−10¹⁵/0.001=−10¹⁸ cm⁻⁴.
Multiply by −qDp=−1.6×10⁻¹⁹×10.
The product is +1.6 A/cm², directed along +x.
solution.explanation: The product is +1.6 A/cm², directed along +x.
commonMistakes: The length in the exponential denominator contributes to the derivative.

hints: Identify the conditions under which hole-profile diffusion current applies.
Start from $ J_p=-qD_p\,dp/dx $.

verification.method: Centered finite-difference gradient of the original profile, then signed hole current. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.

question: A uniform sample has conductivity 1 S/cm, length 1 cm and cross-sectional area 10⁻⁴ cm². Neglect contacts. Find resistance in kΩ.

steps: The sample conductance is σA/L=10⁻⁴ S.
Resistance is its reciprocal, 10⁴ Ω.
Convert to kΩ to obtain 10 kΩ.
solution.explanation: Convert to kΩ to obtain 10 kΩ.
commonMistakes: Conductivity is a material property; conductance also depends on geometry.

hints: Identify the conditions under which bulk conduction geometry applies.

question: In a fully ionized extrinsic regime, hold carrier density fixed and assume μ(T)∝T⁻³ᐟ². Find σ(600 K)/σ(300 K) in this model.

steps: With density fixed, conductivity changes in direct proportion to mobility.
The temperature ratio is 2.
The model gives 2⁻³ᐟ²=1/(2√2)≈0.353553391.
commonMistakes: This model excludes intrinsic-density increase and dopant freeze-out effects.

hints: Identify the conditions under which mobility-limited temperature dependence applies.
Start from $ \sigma_2/\sigma_1=(T_2/T_1)^{-3/2} $.

question: Which statements about low-field semiconductor drift/diffusion models are true?

options.text: A concentration gradient can produce current even when the electric field is zero
Electron particle flux and electron conventional current always point in the same direction
The Einstein relation links mobility and diffusion under nondegenerate equilibrium assumptions
A spatially uniform concentration removes its diffusion term

steps: The gradient term can survive at zero field and vanishes for uniform density.
Multiplying electron particle flux by negative electron charge reverses its direction.
Nondegenerate equilibrium assumptions give D/μ=kT/q. Select A, C and D.
solution.explanation: Nondegenerate equilibrium assumptions give D/μ=kT/q. Select A, C and D.
commonMistakes: The sign convention must follow carrier charge, not just particle motion.

hints: Identify the conditions under which particle flux versus charge current applies.
Start from $ J_n=q n\mu_nE+qD_n\nabla n $.

verification.method: Signed drift/diffusion constitutive laws and stated nondegenerate Einstein assumptions. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.

question: For uniform linear recombination model dΔn/dt=G−Δn/τ with τ>0, which statements hold?

options.text: The steady excess concentration is Gτ for constant generation
With G=0, excess density decays exponentially
τ has units of inverse seconds

steps: Steady balance gives Δn=Gτ.
Setting G=0 leaves a decaying exponential with pole −1/τ.
Since t/τ is dimensionless, τ has units of time. Select A, B and D.
solution.explanation: Since t/τ is dimensionless, τ has units of time. Select A, B and D.
commonMistakes: Lifetime is a time, whereas recombination rate coefficient 1/τ has inverse-time units.

hints: Identify the conditions under which linear carrier continuity applies.
Start from $ \Delta n(t)=G\tau+C e^{-t/\tau} $.

verification.method: Solve continuity steady balance and homogeneous exponent; lifetime dimensional check. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.
